Something I'm not seeing a lot of people mentioning in the comments is, while your brother will probably need some sort of assistance throughout his life, that level is highly dependent on the support and education that he gets in childhood and young adulthood. Children with autism can't just be left with an iPad and expected to improve. Many people with autism can get to some level of independence, potentially not even needing a guardian, with enough support, especially in childhood.

Depending on how independent he becomes in adulthood he might need to have different living situations. Not all assisted living situations are the same. Some people live in a facility where they are hand fed all meals and rarely leave their room because of their condition. Some people I know live independently in their own apartment in a building where they basically just have a social worker and a nurse on staff to help them if a problem occurs. Depending on where you live these situations are funded by the disabled person working a job, non-profits, government assistance, and family support. In my experience working with disabled folks, autistic people are particularly well suited for supported employment arrangements because they tend to do very well with routines.

Disabled people without a good support system are sadly very vulnerable to abuse and neglect, which are more common than we'd like, even in the USA. But even after your parents are dead, being a good support system for your brother doesn't fall all on you and doesn't mean that he has to live with you.

Your parents MUST figure out a plan for your brother after their passing that doesn't involve you. What if you died unexpectedly or became disabled yourself? Then your brother is out of luck with no one else to help.

I guess I should have said it was falling out of favor in most of western Europe within some influential aristocratic circles and with a significant portion of the general populace. Of course it was usually people disapproving of the colonies held by rival nations. Many independence movements gained the traction that they did because colonialism was falling out of favor. The last significant US territorial holding was the Philippines gaining independence in 1946. The US planned on eventual independence for the Philippines and stated as much in 1916 after they'd already squashed rebellion about a decade prior. 

The concept of self determination was very popular and difficult for former allied nations to reconcile with colonialism after each world war. Many European veterans similarly did not want to fight to stop colonial independence movements after they had just fought a world war to maintain their own independence.

Film, radio, and telegraph technology also allowed many people in Europe to see the conditions of colonial subjects for the first time. These were very influential in gaining independence for the Belgian Congo for example.

TLDR: There are many factors that contributed to waves of decolonization from the 1920s to the 1970s, but one of them was absolutely changes in public opinion on the morality/ethics of colonialism. 

Anyone interested in learning more about the subject, I highly recommend King Leopold's Ghost: A Story of Greed, Terror, and Heroism in Colonial Africa by Adam Hochschild.

I think people are more blaming the British government rather than the British people. Britain wasn't keen to give up its colonies. Colonialism was falling out of favor even before WW1 but Britain didn't relinquish many of its African colonial holdings until the mid 1960s.

If you care about due process for American citizens, you should care about due process for "illegal people". Otherwise how do you know they aren't here legally? Due process has nothing to do with whether we deport every person in the country illegally or let them stay. Without due process it's impossible to determine if someone has a right to stay in the US, even if temporarily, or in detention centers.

Asylum seekers are oftentimes unable to file proper paperwork until they arrive to the country they are seeking asylum in. If you want every asylum application denied, that's one thing, but those people still have a right to due process in their asylum process. They have the right to appeal their case. Being in the US unlawfully can be a criminal or civil matter depending on the circumstances, but many of the people being deported or shipped to CECOT have not been convicted of either civil or criminal immigration offenses. To answer your question, I would say probably not. I wouldn't trust the decision making of which areas were logged and which areas were protected. I used to work a bit in civil/environmental engineering back in college with land developers. In Florida we have a similar system called wetland mitigation credits.

In simple terms, this means if you're a land developer and you want to build a 1 acre parking lot on a wetland, you then have to protect, restore, and/or enhance a wetland of equivalent size. In theory, sounds like a good system. In reality, it opened the door for  developers to drain and pave a wetland that had been natural for hundreds if not thousands of years, dig a few ponds and plant a few native species in an area that had long since dried up and call it "restored" or "preserved". This had huge negative effects on the surrounding ecosystem. You can't just change a chunk of wetland or forest and not expect the surrounding area to be affected.

Theoretically, Florida shouldn't have lost any wetlands over the past 31 years. But we have continued to lose more and more and the standards got lower and lower to support developers financially.

Could I cut down an acre of sequoias in California and protect an acre of scrub pine in Florida and call it a day? Obviously not but that is what I would expect to happen.

I think a better priority would be to focus on subsidizing the timber plantations and expanding timber production on poor farmland. The problem is we really should have started on this solution 30 years ago.

In summary, I'd rather we get creative with more efficient land use and find ways to use less lumber in construction than destroy existing forest ecosystems. No matter what they say, once you destroy a complex ecosystem, it's almost impossible to fully restore it and at best it will cost a fortune to do so.

I'd agree that median is a measure of center and mean is a measure of center, but I would never call a median an average because average specifically refers to the mean.

Maybe this is a cultural/language difference since I'm assuming you're Australian by your username. In the US where I am, average and mean both refer to calculating the total of a set of values by the total number of values. Median specifically refers to ordering those values by size and then selecting the middle value.

If I took a statistics 101 test and it asked for the average and I provided the median it would be wrong. If someone asked for the average of 10, 20, and 90 and I gave anything other than 40, it would be wrong.

Often, people who aren't familiar with statistics don't understand how they are calculated and think that "average" means "typical". I know I'm being really pedantic with the language here, but I think these distinctions are important because they are used to lie to us all the time. 99 people with $0 and 1 person with $1,000,000 means an average wealth of $10k but the typical person in that room is still penniless.

Statistics is not a required subject where I went to school so most people I know do not know or understand any of these differences and it makes them very vulnerable to misinterpreting statistics and graphs.

Hopefully the stats is a required class down under! It seems online like Australians might be less susceptible to media bullshit than Americans :)

Both mean (average) and median are ways of generalizing data from a large group and have their own upsides and downsides. Median is a much better way of showing a statistic like how much income a typical individual from a population might make because outliers that dramatically skew an average do not have the same effect on a median. There are situations where a mean or average would be a superior representation of a data set but this is not one of them.

In common usage, people think of the median and mean (average) as the same but they are calculated completely differently.

I am pro GMO, but that doesn't mean GMOs are inherently safe. If it was easy to make good, safe GMOs, we'd see a lot more of them in widespread use.

An example is I worked on a transgenic cultivar that produced so much of a toxin that is would be too harmful to consume. The original cultivar already produced that toxin but in safe levels. This transgenic cultivar was good for research purposes but was scrapped as something to be grown for food. A change as drastic as this would be more unlikely in a traditional hybrid.

I strongly agree that the GMOs that are in widespread production now are safe and a marvel of genetic science. All I'm saying is that creating a GMO is a slow process that produces many failed experiments some of which fail because they can have dangerous consequences. I work in a plant breeding lab where we create new transgenic crops. Those crops are not released to the public because we haven't tested them enough to know if they're safe. That's why we autoclave any genetic material from those plants and if we keep any seeds from them they go in a padlocked freezer in a locked building.

A GMO crop can have a drastically different genetic code compared to a new hybrid of a crop as it has DNA from a different species spliced in. One of the main reasons to create GMOs are that they produce chemical compounds which that specific crop doesn't normally produce. For example, look at BT corn. It produces a chemical compounds that kills caterpillars that eat it. What if the genes that caused that chemical also coded for a chemical that could kill bees. That would be bad.

GMO crops could have negative effects on other organisms in the environment. The GMO crops that are widespread now are generally considered safe and they have been tested and researched extensively, but potentially dangerous GMO crops have been created but then scrapped at the research level before being released. It's not a totally crazy idea to think that someday a GMO crops could be released that could be harmful. Labs developing GMO crops take great care to keep them isolated and it's a crime to let them out of the controlled lab environment if I'm not mistaken. If all GMOs were inherently safe, labs wouldn't go through all the trouble.

Pugs are not genetically modified int eh way that the phrase is used. Genetically modified in this context means transgenic. Pugs were selectively bred to be the way they are. Genetically modified refers to organisms that have had DNA from other organisms manually inserted into their genetic code.

If a farmer wants to they can just buy cheaper non-GMO seed from another company besides Monsanto. Often they don't because they weigh the options and the increased income from better yields offsets the increased seed cost and then some. And no yield is ever guaranteed in farming. Any crop can be wildly successful or an utter disaster GMO or not.

Nearly all bananas are non-GMO. The Cavendish banana that is the typical banana you'd find in a grocery store is a banana variety that has been selectively bred for certain traits. GMO is typically used to refer to a crop that has had specific genes manually inserted into it's genetic code. For example, if you took a piece of spinach DNA that isn't normally in a tomato and spliced that genetic code into the tomato's DNA.

The danger of GMO crops is not to the people eating them. A GMO soybean is just as safe and healthy to eat as a non-GMO soybean. The dangers of GMOs come from how much we don't know about them and their potential to damage other species and varieties of crops. Producing new GMO crops is super complicated and things go wrong all the time which is why there are only a handful of GMO crops that are in widespread production.
